name: Introspection illusion
statement: People treat their own introspections as strong evidence about themselves while judging others by behaviour, and so find bias in others and not in themselves.
meaning: The claim is about an asymmetry, not about accuracy. Pronin sets it out in four parts: heavy weighting of introspection when assessing oneself, absence of that weighting when assessing others, disregard of one's own behaviour that follows from it, and a difference in how much one's own and others' introspections are valued. The last part is what separates the idea from the obvious observation that a person knows their own thoughts better than a stranger does. Pronin's argument is that even when someone hands over a full account of what they were thinking, the listener discounts it and looks at what the person did. The illusion works in both directions. When introspection turns up good intentions, people weigh those intentions. When it turns up nothing, as happens with biases that operate without conscious traces, people weigh the silence as evidence of objectivity. Three neighbouring entries carry material that is often lent to this one and is not repeated here. The older claim that introspective reports about the causes of one's own judgements are often wrong is the premise this framework builds on rather than part of it, and it belongs to confabulation, entry 42, together with the choice blindness experiments. The bias blind spot, the pattern this framework was built to explain, is entry 133. The wider self-other asymmetry in what counts as evidence about a person is the illusion of asymmetric insight, entry 234.

origin.who: Emily Pronin, Thomas Gilovich and Lee Ross
origin.note: The term is coined in this theoretical note, where the authors write that they refer to the asymmetry as the introspection illusion because the faith people have in the validity of their own introspections is misplaced. The note runs no experiment of its own, and it does print results from four papers its reference list gives as manuscripts in preparation. One of those figures carries the strategy data that later became Pronin and Kugler's Study 1. The published experiments came three years later, in Pronin and Kugler's Journal of Experimental Social Psychology paper and in Pronin, Berger and Molouki's five studies of conformity. The fullest statement of the framework is Pronin's 67-page chapter in Advances in Experimental Social Psychology in 2009.

evidence: Two experimental papers carry the case, both published in 2007. Pronin and Kugler ran five studies on Harvard and Princeton undergraduates, with samples of 38 to 247. Study 1 gave 247 Harvard students a description of the self-serving bias, the halo effect or the fundamental attribution error and asked how much they or the average Harvard student showed it. They rated themselves lower, means of 5.05 against 6.83 on a nine-point scale, F(1, 245) = 76.45. Asked which of two strategies they had used, those rating themselves reported weighing thoughts and motives above behaviour, 5.17 against 3.91, while those rating peers reversed it, 3.48 against 6.10, interaction F(1, 244) = 70.31. The more a participant leaned on thoughts rather than behaviour, the less bias they reported, r(247) = -.43. Study 1a asked 83 students which strategy would be valuable rather than which they used, and found the same reversal, interaction F(1, 81) = 17.93. Studies 2 and 3 tested whether the gap is just a matter of access, and they are the two that put a measured behaviour into the analysis. In Study 2, 96 Princeton students rated themselves on four traits after listing their thoughts; 77% of observers said the ratings were affected by the better-than-average effect against 52% of the raters themselves. The degree of self-flattery visible in the ratings predicted observers' judgements, r(62) = .48, but not the raters' own, r(30) = .17. Handing observers the raters' written thoughts changed nothing, including when only the longest reports were analysed. Study 3 repeated this with 81 students who were given a score of 7 correct out of 18 on a bogus social intelligence test, placing them in the 30th percentile, and who then dismissed the test. Their dismissal predicted observers' bias ratings, r(52) = -.34, and not their own, r(25) = -.09. Study 4 had 38 students pick between a thought-based and an action-based definition of bias in eight scenarios: 62% chose the introspective definition for themselves and 51% for another person, F(1, 36) = 4.33. Study 5 gave 78 students a fabricated Science article about nonconscious influences, one further participant being dropped for suspicion, after which the blind spot disappeared, mean 5.88 where 6 marked parity with peers, against 5.29 in the control condition, F(1, 76) = 6.69. Pronin, Berger and Molouki ran five more studies, on perceptions of conformity. Forty-four Princeton undergraduates rated themselves as less swayed than the average student across 16 examples of social influence, t(42) = 4.62. Forty iPod owners did the same after conformity had been framed as either desirable or undesirable, mean 3.30 where 5 marked parity, t(38) = 6.17, and the framing left that denial unchanged, F(1, 38) = 0.52, p = .48. Their Study 3 holds the behaviour fixed. Forty-four students voted on 18 university proposals after being told what a panel of their peers thought, and sided with the panel on a mean of 10.55 against a chance value of 9, t(42) = 4.74. They then judged their own record and a peer's record built to show the same number of agreements. They rated themselves less influenced than that peer, 3.07 against 3.61, F(1, 43) = 6.79, and reported weighing their thoughts above their votes for themselves while weighing the peer's votes and presumed thoughts equally, interaction F(1, 43) = 66.76. Study 4 repeated the design between subjects on 64 Stanford undergraduates, with observers given the actors' written thoughts, and found the same gap, 3.97 against 4.84, F(1, 31) = 6.05. Study 5 had 92 students choose between thought-based and action-based definitions of conformity in three scenarios: 63% chose the introspective definition for themselves and 38% for another person, F(1, 90) = 13.66.

replication.headline: The introspection account has not replicated: a 404-person test found no crossover between self and other, and the mechanism it names explained about 1% of the variance in bias blind spot scores.
replication.detail: Mandel and colleagues tested the strategy result, which they say had not been replicated before theirs, on 404 of the 427 people recruited online, in experiments that were not preregistered. The predicted crossover did not appear. Participants reported using the behavioural strategy more than the introspective one when judging themselves as well as when judging others, d = -0.21, 95% CI [-0.28, -0.14] for self and d = -0.33, 95% CI [-0.40, -0.27] for others. What survives is that the gap is narrower for the self, interaction F(1, 403) = 8.53, p = .004, partial eta-squared = .021. A score built the way Pronin and Kugler built theirs correlated with the blind spot at r = .11, p = .026, about 1% of the variance, and lost significance once cognitive ability and open-minded thinking were entered alongside it. The authors conclude that their results question whether introspection bias is a principal mechanism. Their participants rated self and other in spaced blocks within one session, where Pronin and Kugler assigned each participant to rate one or the other. That difference matters elsewhere. Pronin and Kugler reported in 2010 that 50 Princeton students rated their own past and future decisions as less predictable a priori than a roommate's, 3.86 against 4.81 on a seven-point scale, F(1, 48) = 14.46. They printed no effect size, and the d = -1.08, 95% CI [-1.67, -0.48] usually attached to that experiment is the replicating team's calculation from it. Chandrashekar and colleagues ran three preregistered replications on 1,031 people: d = -0.84, 95% CI [-1.46, -0.23] on 47 Hong Kong students, d = -0.30, 95% CI [-0.66, 0.05] on 126 Americans, and d = -0.33, 95% CI [-0.52, -0.14] in a between-subjects sample of 424. In a within-subjects sample of 434 the effect was d = 0.00, 95% CI [-0.10, 0.10]. Their pooled estimate is d = -0.36, 95% CI [-0.52, -0.20], which they call a mostly successful replication with smaller effects. The asymmetry survives when self and other are rated by different people and vanishes when the same person rates both. A motivational rival has since gained ground. Cruz and Mata ran two preregistered studies, on 100 online workers and 126 students. The blind spot was narrower for biases described as having good consequences than for the same biases described as having bad ones, b = -0.21, SE = 0.09, t = -2.43, p = .015. Their second study did not reproduce that interaction in the preregistered model, t = -1.65, p = .100, and reached it only in an exploratory analysis of variance, F(1, 125) = 5.00, p = .027. A continuous test in the same sample found the blind spot smaller the more desirable a bias was rated, b = -0.21, SE = 0.05, t = -3.78. No preregistered replication of the four components as Pronin states them was located.

study.cite: Mandel, D. R., Collins, R. N., Walker, A. C., Fugelsang, J. A., & Risko, E. F. (2022). Hypothesized drivers of the bias blind spot: Cognitive sophistication, introspection bias, and conversational processes. Judgment and Decision Making, 17(6), 1392-1421.

limits: The framework and its supporting experiments are separable, and the experiments are narrow. Pronin and Kugler's five studies ran on Harvard and Princeton undergraduates with a largest sample of 247, Pronin, Berger and Molouki's ran on Princeton and Stanford undergraduates with a largest sample of 92, and none of the ten was preregistered. The central measure asks people to report which mental strategy they used, which is an introspective report about introspection. Whether a person can meaningfully rate how much they got inside another person's head is a question Mandel and colleagues raise directly. They quote Ehrlinger and colleagues to the effect that people cannot introspect into others' minds by definition, which would make part of the predicted asymmetry a floor rather than a finding. Some of the effects are thin where the design is weakest. The definition asymmetry in Pronin and Kugler's Study 4 rests on 62% against 51% in 38 participants, F(1, 36) = 4.33, p = .04, and the peer half of the Study 1a reversal reached F(1, 39) = 3.77, p = .06 on its own. Pronin's 2009 chapter runs to 67 pages and gathers work across judgement, attitudes, conformity, relationships and prejudice under one heading. Most of that material was designed to test something else, and some of it is unpublished. The chapter's description of a BMW survey by Berger and Pronin, means of 2.70 against 4.93 with t(27) = 4.90, cites unpublished raw data, and is reported here from the chapter rather than from a paper. Pronin's most recent statement of the account, written with Hazel in 2023, rests it on the 2007 paper, and a search of that review's text for the name Mandel returns nothing. Searches ran on 17 August 2026 across Crossref, Unpaywall, Europe PMC, PubMed Central, the Judgment and Decision Making archive and the open web. Pronin and Kugler's 2007 and 2010 papers, Pronin, Berger and Molouki's 2007 paper, Pronin's 2009 chapter, Pronin, Gilovich and Ross's 2004 note, Pronin and Hazel's 2023 review, Mandel and colleagues' paper, both papers by Chandrashekar and colleagues, Cruz and Mata's paper and Wilson and Dunn's review were read in full. Every figure quoted here was taken from two independent downloads of the document it comes from. Wilson and Dunn support the premise rather than the asymmetry: they state that introspection cannot provide a direct pipeline to nonconscious processes, and that seeing ourselves through the eyes of others and observing our own behaviour are among the alternatives. The copy of that review read here is the Reviews in Advance version, paginated 17.1 to 17.26 rather than 493 to 518.
misreadings: Choice blindness is offered as the experimental proof of the introspection illusion, and it is not evidence for the claim Pronin makes. Switch the outcome of a choice and most people justify the option they rejected. That literature, with its full range of detection rates, is set out under confabulation, entry 42. It establishes that people fail to notice a switched outcome and then explain the switched one, which is a claim about the reliability of introspective reports. It says nothing about whether people weigh their own introspections more heavily than other people's. Pronin's 2009 chapter, the fullest statement of the framework, cites no choice blindness work: the phrase does not appear in its text, and searches of that text for Johansson, Hall, Sikström, Tärning and Olsson return nothing. The second misreading is chronological. The term is often credited to the 2007 experiments, and it was coined in the 2004 theoretical note. The third is to treat the introspection illusion as established because the bias blind spot is. The blind spot has its own replication record, at entry 133, and that record is strong. The introspection account is one of several proposed explanations for it, and the paper that tested three of them preferred a conversational-artefact account. On that reading the questionnaire tells participants in advance that the biases are real and common, which licenses a high rating for other people.
